doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Finding your own sound: influences from Hackett to Maynard Ferguson
summary: He names the players he absorbed, from Bobby Hackett, Lee Morgan and Clifford to Miles and Maynard, and prefers ballads to high, loud, fast playing.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: how you had to be an individual. How you had to create your own sound. That’s the case with me and the people that I worked with back in the day. When you heard Conrad Gozzo playing lead you knew it was Conrad Gozzo you know. When you heard Conte Candoli playing a solo, you knew it was Conte Candoli. You heard Pete Candoli you knew it was Pete Candoli. You know it’s just — Plas Johnson, you knew it was Plas Johnson. I listened to everybody and I picked up everybody from playing records and records and sitting next to them and playing and picking up their little innuendoes and a little of this, a little of that, a little of that, and I picked it all up and I put it all together and then I became myself. And when you become yourself then you have a signature. And so I listened to Lee Morgan, I listened to Kenny Dorham, I listened to — after Bobby Hackett this is. But Bobby Hackett was the one that got me playing like lyrical and tunes and stuff like that. And then I listened to Lee Morgan and like I said, and Nat Adderley I listened to as well. And then oh there were so many people. And of course Clifford and Miles. And you know for what it’s worth when I was playing and I heard Miles, Miles did not touch me like Clifford did or Lee Morgan or Kenny Dorham, players like Charlie Shavers — there was something about that. Miles was different, completely different. His own signature. And I didn’t understand that then. But then the next person was Maynard Ferguson. And talking about a culture shock — because these records my brother had you know and I would play along with all these records. And my brother’s on the road and I’m upstairs in our house in Mayfield Heights in the suburbs of Cleveland playing along with these records. Well I’d go from cornet to trumpet and now I’m trying to play along with Maynard. Well I’ll tell ya, he made me work really hard but I got it you know, and I got it and I was able to do it and play along with his records. Play “Maria” and play all these different things. And so like I said, three things I don’t like to do is play high, loud and fast. Those are three things I don’t like to do. When I want to hear a person’s soul and hear them play, have them play me a ballad and then I’ll know who they are. Because you can’t tell who they are when they’re playing like — well we did that “Cherokee” with Arturo Sandoval and I mean how can you tell a person’s — what their soul is like when you hear that? I mean it’s just notes that are flying by a mile a minute you know, and then high notes. It doesn’t tell you anything.
